title: Opus 5.5 (High) is your Project Manager
author: lastplankgames
selftext:
I wanted to add some advice here from my own experience. If you’re using a single instance of Claude to do all of your work, you’re wasting tokens and your own time.

Picture a game dev team: it’s not one person doing everything. You’d usually have someone on game logic, someone on art, music, sound effects, story, etc. Claude works the same way. Run Opus 5.5 on medium/high as the lead, and have it spin up agents on Sonnet medium/high. You deal with Opus, and Opus delegates the work and reviews what the agents under it produce.

What this means is you get Sonnet-quality work (which is mostly fine), but with an Opus review on top that sends it back until Opus thinks it’s good enough. Opus then gives you a summary report on what each agent has done. This has massively sped up my output. Opus has become a reliable partner: it gives me good summaries and keeps the lower agents in check.

**Keeping token usage down!**

A session sitting at 300k context costs a lot more per call than a fresh one, so the bill is mostly context size × number of calls. A few things that made a big difference for me:

Handoffs. When the lead (Opus) gets to around 300k context, it writes everything down: a board file with what’s in flight, who’s on what and what I’m waiting on, plus a short handoff note with lessons learned. Then it clears itself and the next “PM” reads those files and carries on. Nothing gets lost, because the state lives in files, not in the chat.

Clear the agents after every task. Each Sonnet agent does one job, reports back, then gets wiped and given a fresh brief for the next one. One of mine once got to 400k+ doing three jobs in a row, which is just burning money.

Short reports. Agents start every report with one status line (done / blocked / needs review, test results, the question). The details go in a file the lead reads only if it needs to. That stops Opus paging through long transcripts.

Cheap models for grunt work. Searching the codebase or digging through logs goes to a Haiku sub-agent. It’s a fraction of the price and only the answer comes back.

Right effort for the job. Mechanical stuff (renames, wiring in approved art) runs on low effort, normal work on medium, and only tricky infra bugs get high. Don’t switch the model or effort mid-session either, it throws away the cache.

Pictures, not piles of screenshots. Reviews use one labelled contact sheet instead of ten full-size screenshots. Same for videos: a grid of frames instead of the clip.

It sounds like a lot of setup, but once it’s running you’re basically just talking to one lead who manages the team for you.

I'll make it easy for you guys.

"Use fable to plan and audit. use opus 5.5 as the output agent for all created documentation. Use opus 5.5 at medium effort at the most for difficult tasks and sonnet for the rest."

replies.body: idk about that i tried fable last week with the free resets and it blew through tokens. i think where I'm at, given that my game is probably not too complex, is opus5.5 medium with delegation to sonnet and haiku, and then the very rare thing that doesn't get done properly i will send to fable.

replies.author: Ohgood9002
replies.body:
When you delegate fable to only be an audit and plan role you get the benefits of it's better reasoning without the usage cost.  The sub agents handle the repeated coding and documentation tasks that normally would burn through Fable usage like a wildfire. 

I have 2 claude pro accounts and hit my weekly on both of them while my fable didn't even need to be reset with the free resets. 

https://i.redd.it/yd7dz5o2an1i1.png

Okay, well one of them hit the weekly limit. I'll hit the other limit by tomorrow. But fable still won't hit it's limit by then either

comments.author: ChadSexman
comments.body: I find that single session is fine if you keep context in relevant .md and skills. Then set autocompact to 300-500k.

replies.author: lastplankgames
replies.body: Auto compact has been proven to worsen precision and code quality. It consumes context overhead and fine details are missed during the compacting.

replies.author: ChadSexman
replies.body:
Can you give examples of what you mean by “fine details”?

I’ve had no issues with precision or token spend using a single session. Your solution to me feels over-engineered.

replies.author: lastplankgames
replies.body:
It's during the compression. The summary it creates has to be short, so it will sometimes throw away "exact data" to fit the summary it will use to continue. For example, it will not remember the exact code change it made, but rather make a note "the boss damage was changed to x" but won't take into account anything else or exact variable names that were changed to enact that code change.

That's why clearing and handoff.md docs are so important when using /clear and starting from fresh.

comments.author: Braunb8888
comments.body: How do you have it. Create other agents? What is sonnet? Do you have to pay for that as well? I’ve been wondering how to improve the production time.

replies.author: MFour_Sherman
replies.body: Sonnet is a lower tiered engine inside Claude

replies.author: lastplankgames
replies.body:
Simply ask to opus 5.5 "You are PM, you are to spin up 3 engineers at sonnet medium to complete tasks of x, y, z. You will review, feedback, and iterate their work before giving me a summary of their work. Apply you're judgement, and once it's passed all checks - give me a summary for review".

How many agents you can have at once depends on your local PC specs, what engine you're using, etc.

replies.author: Braunb8888
replies.body: How would I know how many I can run?

replies.author: lastplankgames
replies.body: Scarily, it will know your ram, VRAM, and CPU usage and calculate how many agents testing/working will be right for your PC.

comments.author: dank_summers
comments.body: Meh, I definitely notice a step up in quality when I use fable for blender assets

comments.author: throwaway09234023322
comments.body: Hmmm. I'm not sure. I use a coordinator to run agents in parallel. However, I'm not sure that it is really the most efficient workflow. I think you get better token efficiency by having a solo worker (and a separate reviewer to catch errors) do each task with starting a new chat for each task. This removes the overhead of coordination and merge conflicts. Depending on your plan, it could be best to stick with a solo agent.

replies.author: lastplankgames
replies.body: Using fable 5.2 to look up functions, variables, logic, scan through code is a waste of time. In my opinion, it excels at managing and review. If you have loads of money, by all means please use it but opus is golden for PM. I do use Fable for big picture/future feature work but it's like using a nuclear weapon when a bunker buster will do.

replies.author: throwaway09234023322
replies.body:
Yeah, but what information is fable losing by having haiku do a lookup instead? I feel like the savings could be less than you think or paid for with lower quality. Just my opinion but I don't have any hard data on it.

I use opus as coordinator with a couple agents in parallel and fable as reviewer at the moment.

replies.author: lastplankgames
replies.body: It's not, use haiku for the grunt stuff. Fable, in my opinion, should be in a kind of CEO role. Haiku is more than capable to do simple coding, finding functions, etc and reporting that back to fable/opus. Having a behemoth like fable doing simple things like that will cost in the long run.

replies.author: throwaway09234023322
replies.body:
With almost any code change, there is a possibility that something else broke or the change had an unintended consequence. Fable would most likely have caught this type of thing while haiku wouldn't.

I agree with fable being CEO. You probably get the most value with having it review your project occassionally and writing the plan. Fable has caught some major architectural flaws that Opus overlooked, so definitely worth using it for that occassionally imo.

replies.author: lastplankgames
replies.body: Of course, but that is where testing comes in clutch. Having sonnet run their own tests, opus reviewing - I've found less issues this way.

replies.author: LucidFir
replies.body:
I've had it both ways and I'm still not sure what's the best approach. I've had opus delegate a task, and the agent fuck it up, so it's had to be redone to the point where just having opus do it would have been better. This is especially the case because I'm not a coder and opus will know enough to cover my many knowledge gaps and by doing the grunt tasks find bugs and mistakes and fix them without asking and tell me after. I've also had it work perfectly where it sends a bunch of agents to do basic tasks and then check them... but unless i made 2 repos and started 2 chats with the same prompts idk how i could really tell the difference. 

As it is, for me, new chats each feedback and comprehensive note taking in specific documents is working great. at one point sonnet deleted my tutorial intro due to confusion about terms, so now there's a style.md that includes terms. i tried fable last week and it's expensive overkill, except that opus failed to make tunnels twice and fable got it first time. so where I'm at is opus medium with delegation and much documentation, and fable for any failed task.

... glad i wrote this out actually, i think i need fable to fix my multiplayer. it works but it's ugly

replies.author: UncleJoesLandscaping
replies.body: This is basically how I do it. I keep highly related tasks in one chat and start a new chat when there is a new topic. I only use Opus 5.5 and seldom run out of tokens on the $20 plan.

comments.author: Affectionate_Fact854
comments.body:
I'm experimenting with a new method 
So far so good 

I'm on a ultra plan 
And my process is

I set up 
Fable as main orchestrator( communication bridge, plan execution and informs me of open questions, progress and communicates with the team) 

Team is 3 sub orchestrators opus 5.5

Visual,ui and sound studio 

Quality assurance studio 

Backend studio 


Each has their own specialized tasks 

They have a rule they may use sub agents, but subagents may not spawn additional 

If studios agents are done 
The studio communicates with fable, that then sends information to the other studios 

This method there's constant communication and awareness between tasks being done

From my side 
I give documentation to fable 
I'll take screenshots
And show fable what it is, to what I expect 

I will give fable the answers to open questions to steer 
Aswell as I frequently spot check the actual code in the project to see if boiler plate scripts are up to standard 

I'll do my playtests and also give my analysis reports frequently if I am not busy drawing the games art while it's actually working

OR

I would code a example script of what I'm expecting to have to what it currently has 

"This way I'm in full steer control "
*Teams is working 
*Defects is automatically picked up and resolved 
*Tests keeps running 
*art isn't being backlogged because I can actually put in the time to make it without constant interaction

Token usage is not bad 6hours of this workflow with no stops cost me roughly 12% of the weekly quota

comments.author: pigeon_shit
comments.body:
I did a test yesterday. Cowork main project with all the folders, Cowork new project with just 1 folder, Code on desktop with just 1 folder, and Code via powershell. comments.author: Jaskkro

comments.author: OneMoreFightGame
comments.body: Having the model pass on a list of notes and starting a new chat fresh has helped me SO much with my usage. It's such an obvious move that took me too long to learn. I'm sure it'll end up benefitting someone else too

comments.author: Arcodiant
comments.body: Orchestration isn't really an ideal task for Opus, as it's a long-running session with a large history to keep in context - and therefore token-heavy and potentially expensive - and it's not making decisions so much as kicking off subagents with specific direction. Use Sonnet as your orchestrator, and have it run an Opus subagent to do research or make complex decisions and plans - then pass that to another Sonnet subagent to execute. I usually run an Opus agent up front to plan the task list and save it to a bunch of markdown files; then the orchestrator passes each file to a researcher/planner and then a series of implementors, choosing models as it goes.
